c0006: Equivalent covers per day, year-1 average: about 60 dine-in (patio included from April through October) and about 55 from take-out, pickup and delivery marketplaces, which are the orders divided by the average check. A Saturday runs well above the average and a Tuesday well below it (Kit estimate). Compare it with the foot traffic on your street on a Friday night and a Tuesday at lunch, and with your own test orders
c0008: Per cover, EXCL. sales tax and tip: an order of street tacos, some quesadilla or gringa, chips & guac or a side, and a drink or so add up to about $17.50. The example uses a street taco at $4.00 on the menu (2.6 tacos per cover), a quesadilla or gringa at $11.50, chips & guac or sides at $7.00 and drinks at $3.60 (Kit estimate). Street tacos run $3.00-3.75 on casual menus in mid-size cities (menus read in October 2026). The "Menu price incl. sales tax (calculated)" row below shows the price with your local rate applied
c0010: 365 days minus 52 closed Mondays, the main holidays (Thanksgiving, Christmas, New Year's Day, July 4) and one inventory day, rounded to 308. It is the SAME figure for the P&L, break-even, scenarios and staffing hours
c0012: Repeat neighborhood regulars and more pickup in year 2. It applies to covers at the same average check; staffing does NOT rise with this percentage: it comes from the "Staffing" tab
c0014: On top of year 2. Conservative: the ceiling is set by the trompos, the griddle and the 30 seats on Friday and Saturday nights
c0022: Cost of goods sold on food sales: the menu averages about 25% of menu price (street tacos and quesadillas about 25%, chips & guac about 28% depending on the avocado, birria about 30%), plus 1.5 points of waste (leftover cone from the trompo and cut salsas that get thrown out) and a little prudence, because meat and tortilla prices are Kit estimates. Cost each taco with the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator
c0024: Weighted average of aguas frescas, sodas, water, Mexican beer and wine against their menu prices: aguas frescas and sodas cost a small share of their price, while beer and wine run higher and pull the average up. If your beer distributor lends you the tap equipment, get the keg price in writing
c0026: Clamshells, foil, salsa cups, bags, paper, napkins and gloves for everything that leaves the shop, plus take-out containers for leftovers. Some cities and states restrict foam and single-use plastics or require utensils only on request: check your local packaging ordinances
c0028: Sales through third-party delivery marketplaces (DoorDash, Uber Eats, Grubhub) as a share of total sales. Counter orders, pickup and direct phone or web orders pay no commission and do not go here. Tortillas travel worse than other dishes: a build-your-own order (meat, tortillas and toppings packed separately) holds up, but do not go above this share without testing it
c0030: The example uses 25%, a Plus plan on DoorDash or Uber Eats (the Basic plan is about 15% with little visibility, Premier is 30%, and app pickup orders add 6-10%). Check your contract. If you deliver yourself, enter 0 and add the driver to the "Staffing" tab as a W-2 employee, with hired and non-owned auto insurance (check your state)
c0042: About 1,200 sq ft (111 sq m) with a hood and exhaust route to the roof possible (that is the filter for the space): a counter-service dining room with 30 seats, an open kitchen with the trompos, the griddle and the comal, restrooms (one ADA-accessible) and storage, on a street with steady foot traffic near a campus or a nightlife area in a mid-size city, second-generation space with no key money: about $28 per sq ft a year (Kit estimate, editable). The weight of rent on sales is calculated by the workbook itself in the rent row of the "3-Year P&L"
c0044: Security deposit, in months of rent. The example uses two; commercial leases commonly ask for one to three, and some landlords also want a personal guarantee: check it with your attorney
c0046: Electricity (refrigeration, exhaust, HVAC and the dish machine), the gas for the vertical broilers, the griddle, the comal and the range, and water. Ask the landlord for the space's utility history
c0048: General liability, liquor liability (beer & wine), property coverage with equipment breakdown for the refrigeration, and workers' comp. Tell the carrier you cook with gas vertical broilers, a griddle and a fryer: it changes the premium and the terms. Rates vary by state, so get at least two quotes
c0057: Nominal annual rate, not APR. The example uses 10%. Ask two lenders for a quote before you set it; the refrigeration and the kitchen equipment can also be financed through equipment financing or a lease: compare
c0061: Years you pay interest only before principal repayment starts. The example uses 0, because SBA 7(a) loans amortize from the start. A year of interest only can ease the build-out and the first months of trading: ask your lender, and check the cash slack of the first repayment year on the "Break-Even" tab
c0063: Three months of fixed costs: the cushion for the ramp-up, which with Month 1 in January falls on the slowest months of the year (January and February)
c0072: One sales tax rate for the whole example (8%: state plus local, so look up yours). In this workbook it also applies to alcohol sold to go, and it equals the on-site rate, so the two rows give the same result. There is no input credit: the workbook does not recover sales tax on purchases, so that row is 0. Some states tax food to go differently, so check yours. Utilities, equipment and services use the rate in the cell below
c0079: Build-out, Type I hood and exhaust, electrical service, plumbing, gas lines, HVAC, signage and facade. A 10-year straight-line life for the model; your tax depreciation schedule may differ (MACRS, Section 179), so confirm it with your CPA
c0081: Vertical broilers, griddle and comal, fryer, walk-in and refrigeration, dish machine, furniture and POS: a 7-year straight-line life for the model; your tax depreciation schedule may differ, so confirm it with your CPA
c0088: Dining room seats. The patio adds 12 seats from April through October, with its own city patio permit, and guests who take their tacos to go or receive them at home do not use a seat: that is why the seat turns in the row above are higher than the real turns of your dining room
c0090: A new taqueria draws the curious in the first month, but a regular base takes a quarter to build: Month 1 (January) bills 75% of what it will bill at four months. At 100% the ramp is removed
c0092: Four months to reach full pace: January through April, so you reach the spring patio season with a customer base
c0094: Two months of rent before opening: the build-out, the hood and exhaust route and the permits. If the lender funds the loan when build-out starts, add the interest for those months, which this workbook does not count, and remember that your repayment schedule starts at closing
c0096: Cushion on the build-out and fixtures, which is where the surprises show up (the exhaust route to the roof, the gas lines, the grease interceptor). A lender will not finance a remodel without one
c0099: Weighted average: dine-in and pickup are paid at once, and the delivery marketplaces pay out what they sell every few days (15% of sales in this example)
c0101: Payment terms with your meat, tortilla, produce and beverage suppliers: what they finance for you. New accounts often start on COD, and terms are the first thing you lose if you pay late
c0103: Month of the 12-Month Cash Flow in which a summer extra payment falls. It only matters if you enter more than 12 pay periods; with 12 there are no extra payments. If you use it, July is Month 7, because Month 1 of the plan is January
c0105: Month of the 12-Month Cash Flow in which a holiday extra payment falls. It only matters if you enter more than 12 pay periods; with 12 there are no extra payments. If you use it, December is Month 12, because Month 1 of the plan is January
c0118: Your state or local minimum wage as an annual full-time figure (hourly rate × 2,080 hours), if it is higher than the federal $7.25 an hour. With 0, the traffic light compares only against the federal floor
c0145: Drawings for the build-out and the hood, plan review and permit fees. The beer & wine license varies widely by state in cost and timing: ask your state agency early and add your own quote; this line does not assume one
c0148: Kitchen with washable wall finish and slip-resistant floor, restrooms (one ADA-accessible), ceilings and acoustic treatment, the counter and service line, plus signage and facade (about $4,000). Kit estimate: get two bids
c0150: A Type I hood of 10-12 ft with UL 300 fire suppression and makeup air over the griddle, the fryer and the gas vertical broilers. Hood packages run $5,000-$25,000 and the example budgets $22,000. A charcoal trompo is a solid-fuel appliance (NFPA 96: its own exhaust, a spark arrestor and daily ash removal), so it is a variant, not the example. No manufacturer posts a price per foot: ask your mechanical contractor for a quote with your drawings, and ask the fire marshal in writing
c0152: Electrical service and panel for the refrigeration, exhaust, HVAC and dish machine, plus the gas lines to the broilers, the griddle and the range. Ask for the available electrical and gas capacity BEFORE you sign the lease: a new service from the utility can take weeks or months
c0154: Hot and cold water in the kitchen, drains with a grease interceptor ($3,500-$7,500), HVAC for the dining room and exhaust with makeup air for the support kitchen
c0156: Two gas vertical broilers: one for the al pastor and a second cone or backup. WebstaurantStore lists the Avantco VB203 at $999 and the Visvardis DG8A at $2,844 (Oct 2026); cones run about 30 lb (13.6 kg). The example budgets the pair plus trays, slicing knives and a pineapple holder. A charcoal trompo is a solid-fuel variant (NFPA 96)
c0158: A 36 in (91 cm) flat-top griddle for the meats and a comal to warm the tortillas. At WebstaurantStore a Vulcan VCRG36-M1 lists at $2,501 and a Star 636MF at $2,129 (Oct 2026); the comal is Kit estimate: get a quote
c0160: Fryer for the chips, stock-pot range for the carnitas and guisados, a 4-well steam table (listings start around $1,119) and tortilla warmers. Kit estimate
c0162: A 6×8 ft (1.8×2.4 m) walk-in cooler for the marinated meat in volume. A Norlake Kold Locker lists at $12,808 (WebstaurantStore, Oct 2026)
c0164: Refrigerated prep table for the garnishes, a refrigerated salsa bar and a freezer. No salsa bar price was read, so it is a Kit estimate: get two quotes
c0168: Hotel pans, blenders for the salsas, probe thermometers, scales, dishware and baskets, manual tortilla presses (a Choice 7½ in (19 cm) press lists at $17.49), the required public notices (health permit, beer & wine license, labor law posters) and allergen signs (the 9 major allergens, including sesame: salsa macha = peanuts + sesame; flour tortillas = wheat). Food handler cards and the CFPM exam are budgeted in the P&L
c0170: Beer cooler and agua fresca dispensers. Kit estimate. If your beer distributor lends you the tap equipment, this line goes down
c0172: Tables and chairs for 30 seats in the dining room and 12 on the seasonal patio (April through October)
c0179: Brand identity, a website with the menu and online ordering, a photo shoot and the opening campaign
c0181: Meat, dried chiles and imported Mexican specialty products (ask for lead times: they can take weeks), corn tortillas, beer and wine, soft drinks and the take-out packaging
c0215: Tacos, gringas and quesadillas, plates and sides: about 52% dine-in, about 33% direct pickup and 15% through delivery marketplaces. One sales tax rate in the example, whether guests eat in or take it to go; some states tax food to go differently, so check yours
c0231: The monthly amount is on the "0. Assumptions" tab; here it is multiplied by twelve. The two months of rent before opening are on "Startup Costs" and are NOT counted twice
c0241: Hood and duct cleaning on the schedule that NFPA 96 and your local authority require, service for the gas vertical broilers, griddle and range, and the refrigeration technician
c0243: Google Business Profile, Yelp, social media, seasonal photos and promotions (Cinco de Mayo, Mexican Independence Day in September, Day of the Dead in November); the opening campaign is in "Startup Costs"
c0245: POS subscription, online ordering, the delivery marketplace tablets, phone and internet
c0247: Cleaning supplies, uniform and towel laundry, gloves and any lab tests or records your written food safety plan calls for
c0249: Licensed hauler for trash, cardboard, used cooking oil and grease, plus annual permit renewals. If your city charges a patio or sidewalk café permit fee, add it here: this plan has not read any city fee schedule, so enter your city's own
c0255: CFPM certification and food handler cards, allergen training and OSHA basics for every employee: burns from the griddle and the fryer, cuts when slicing the trompo, gas and heat
c0279: Floor for the margin after ALL variable costs (cost of goods sold, packaging, delivery marketplaces, card fees and miscellaneous). With cost of goods sold alone, a taqueria keeps a much higher margin. Kit estimate
c0282: Ceiling for cost of goods sold on sales: the al pastor taco runs well below it, while carnitas, suadero, barbacoa, birria and avocado push it up. Kit estimate
c0284: Ceiling for labor on sales with two taqueros and counter service. Kit estimate
c0288: Floor for steady-state net income so the plan holds up: 5% of sales. A well-run taqueria earns more, but this is a realistic floor, not a hope. Kit estimate
c0322: Full seatings per seat per day you can run, counting the take-out and delivery orders, which do not take a seat (almost half the covers in the example): about 3 dine-in turns in counter service (lunch and dinner, stays of 20-30 minutes) plus about 2 for take-out and delivery per seat. It is the physical ceiling of the space, not a target
c0363: Marinates and builds the trompo, runs the cutting on the busy shift, buys (the dried chile and Mexican specialty distributor included) and manages. The workbook imputes a monthly salary as if on payroll, which is the prudent side; confirm with your CPA how you will pay yourself (owner's draw or W-2 under an S corp). The example pays the owner below a manager: owner's draw in addition from net profit
c0365: Slices the trompo, runs the griddle and the comal and can marinate with the owner. It is an investment, not an expense: if only the owner can marinate and slice the trompo, a sick day closes the shop
c0367: Carnitas and guisados, salsas, aguas frescas, marinades, mise en place and prep, 30 hours a week
c0369: Year-round: counter, register, take-out orders, the delivery marketplace tablets and allergen information
c0371: Dinner and weekend shifts at the counter and expo, when the shop fills. Part-time W-2 employees; tips are not modeled
c0373: Friday-to-Sunday help: dish, prep and the pickup counter, plus the patio in season. This plan has NO delivery drivers of its own: if you add them, they are W-2 employees in most states, never independent contractors by default (check yours), and you need hired and non-owned auto insurance
c0389: Hours the shop is open to the public, adding the lunch and dinner rushes and the preparation for each. Any slow stretch between the two is not counted
c0391: Average number of people on at once between the trompo, the griddle or comal, the counter and expo. On Saturday night five are needed: the weekend help and the dinner counter staff come in (the annual schedule does not see this: put it on the shift schedule)
c0393: Next-day marinade, building the cone, carnitas and guisados, salsas and mise en place before opening
c0395: The owner with the prep cook. Closing, cleaning and purchasing are outside this schedule: they are the margin between the hours hired and the hours needed
c0411: 4. All figures are EXCL. SALES TAX. To turn a menu price into a price excl. sales tax, divide it by 1 plus your sales tax rate (a rate of 8% means dividing by 1.08). The example uses ONE rate for everything: dine-in, take-out, delivery and beverages; some states tax food to go or alcohol differently, so check yours. The P&L is excl. sales tax; the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab shows what you actually collect, sales tax included, and the sales tax you remit as a quarterly filer.
c0413: 6. The "12-Month Cash Flow" tab answers the question that decides a bank deal: in which month the cash runs out. Its Month 1 is JANUARY, in calendar order: the ramp-up falls on January and February, the slowest months, and that is why working capital counts. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row. The minimum balance of the year can never show in red.
c0415: 8. The Word business plan in this pack quotes the figures in this Excel: if you change a green cell, the Excel rules. The Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator is separate and is used to measure the yield of the cone and COST each taco: do not copy the food cost of one taco into the "0. Assumptions" tab. The "Cost of goods sold on FOOD sales" cell is the weighted average of the WHOLE menu (tacos, gringas, guisados, guacamole and desserts, each by what it sells) plus waste, and that is why it comes out higher than the food cost of the al pastor taco. With the costing of your own menu, check that this average holds.
c0436: In calendar order: the ramp-up falls on the slowest months and working capital covers it. If you open in another month, rotate the seasonality row of the "12-Month Cash Flow" tab
c0438: $3.00-3.75 in mid-size cities; about $5 in big cities
c0440: This plan prices it at $4.00 (a plate of 3 tacos with rice & beans comes to about $14)
c0442: About 25% of its price excl. sales tax
c0443: Kit estimate (Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator)
c0444: 2 corn tortillas (6 in), 1.5 oz (43 g) of meat served, garnish and salsa, with 5% waste. Meat and tortilla prices are Kit estimates: enter your distributor's
c0446: About 7 tacos per raw lb (a 30 lb (13.6 kg) cone is about 208 tacos)
c0448: Measure your own with the Taco Cost & Trompo Yield Calculator (raw cone, leftover, served)
c0450: webstaurantstore.com (Avantco VB203, Visvardis DG8A), read Oct 2026
c0451: The example counts two gas trompos; a charcoal trompo is a solid-fuel variant (NFPA 96)
c0455: This plan: 25% on the 15% of sales that go through marketplaces. Direct pickup pays no commission; check your contract
c0458: Kit example: look up your state and city rate
c0459: One rate in the workbook; some states tax food to go differently
c0461: ≥ 135 °F (57 °C) hot, ≤ 41 °F (5 °C) cold; reheat to 165 °F (74 °C) within 2 h; TPHC up to 4 h with a written procedure
c0463: Each state adopts its own edition. A salsa bar run on TPHC needs the written procedure. Cut tomatoes (pico de gallo, fresh salsas) are TCS; for guacamole, treat it as TCS and ask your regulator
c0467: This plan budgets at least $15/h; enter your state's floor on "0. Assumptions"
c0471: Counter service lands at the low end; two taqueros (the owner and a second one) are insurance, not a luxury
c0475: The threshold of the P&L traffic light; a space with a Type I hood already installed saves build-out
c0477: Set by your county: 145 °F (63 °C) in some, 155 °F (68 °C) in others (165 °F (74 °C) for chicken)
c0479: Ask your health department in writing for the cook temperature, the maximum time on the broiler and what to do with the leftover cone; never rely on a single figure
c0518: Each sales line at ITS rate, read from the sales tax column of the P&L. The example uses one rate for everything, so alcohol to go carries the same rate as dine-in; the share of beverages taxed at the alcohol rate is set in column H of its line on the P&L
